big: Rohan invests ₹1.5 lakh in a tax-saving fund and expects to pay less tax. But he chose the new regime, which does not allow that deduction. His effort saved nothing.

lines: Which regime should I pick? Everyone tells me something different.
Work out both for your own numbers. The old regime allows many deductions. The new one has different slabs. Whichever gives the lower bill for you, wins.

rows: More deductions allowed, with their own conditions
Different slab rates, with fewer deductions
An amount the law lets you subtract from income
A tax-saving fund with a three-year lock-in
note: Rules and limits change with Budgets. Compare both regimes each year, using the current rules.

title: Regimes and filing
stops: You can compare both regimes before choosing
A tax-saving fund helps in every regime
ELSS units cannot be redeemed for three years
Missing the due date has no cost
caps: Work out the tax both ways and pick the lower bill.
Some deductions apply only under the old regime.
ELSS has a lock-in of three years from each investment.
A late return can cost a penalty, and the loss carry-forward.

q: Meena earns a lot but has few deductions. Which step is wise?
opts: Pick the regime her friend chose
Pick the old regime, since it is older
Skip filing since she has few deductions
Work out her tax in both regimes
why: A friend's case can differ from hers, so copying is risky.
Age of a regime does not decide which one is cheaper for her.
Filing is needed, whatever her deductions may be.
Her own numbers decide which regime costs her less.

q: Rohan invests in an ELSS fund. When can he sell those units?
opts: Whenever he likes, at any point
After one month of holding it
why: He cannot sell within the lock-in, so 'whenever' is wrong.
ELSS units have a three-year lock-in from the date of investment.
A month falls well inside the lock-in, so he cannot sell yet.
The lock-in ends after three years, not at retirement.

q: Meena is in the new regime. Does an ELSS investment cut her tax under the old-regime deduction?
opts: No, only the old regime allows it
Yes, in every regime without exception
Yes, but only after five years
Only if she tells her bank first
why: That deduction applies only if she chooses the old regime.
Deductions differ between regimes, so not every regime allows it.
The time period is not what decides this. The regime is.
Her bank does not decide which deduction she gets.

q: Rohan has a loss to carry forward but files his return after the due date. What may happen?
opts: Nothing, since the due date is only a suggestion
The loss is paid back to him in cash
He may lose the right to carry the loss forward
The loss turns into a gain
why: The due date has real effects, and not only a penalty.
A tax loss is not paid back to him in cash form.
Carry forward usually needs a return filed on time.
A loss does not turn into a gain by itself, ever.

pts: Compare both regimes with your own numbers each year.
A deduction helps only if your regime allows it. ELSS locks in for three years.
File on time. A late return can cost a penalty and the loss carry-forward.
